title: LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and NULL
summary: SQL can combine several rules to choose rows. Operators such as AND and OR connect those rules.
introduction: SQL can combine several rules to choose rows. Operators such as AND and OR connect those rules. Find books that are short and cheap, or books from either of two groups. Read each rule aloud before running it.
learningObjectives: Match text patterns with LIKE and the % and _ wildcards
Test membership in a list with IN and NOT IN
Test for missing values with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

blocks.text: `LIKE` compares a text value against a pattern. `%` matches any sequence of characters (including none) and `_` matches exactly one character. Names starting with G:

blocks.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'G%';

blocks.content:
name
----------------
Grace Hopper
Guido van Rossum

blocks.text: A `%` at both ends finds the text anywhere. SQLite's `LIKE` ignores case for ASCII letters, so `'%note%'` matches both `Notebook` and `Sticky notes`:

blocks.code: SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%note%';

blocks.title: LIKE and case by dialect
blocks.text: PostgreSQL's `LIKE` is case-sensitive (it would return only `Sticky notes`); use `ILIKE` there for a case-insensitive match. MySQL follows the column's collation, which is usually case-insensitive. SQLite is case-insensitive for ASCII letters only. When behaviour must be identical everywhere, compare `LOWER(name) LIKE '%note%'`.
`_` is useful for fixed-length codes. Countries written as a `U` plus exactly one more letter:

blocks.code: SELECT name, country FROM customers WHERE country LIKE 'U_';

blocks.content:
name              | country
------------------+--------
Ada Lovelace      | UK
Grace Hopper      | US
Margaret Hamilton | US

blocks.text: `IN` tests whether a value appears in a list, replacing a chain of `OR` conditions. `NOT IN` keeps the rows that match none of the values. The list can also come from a subquery, as shown in [Subqueries](/tutorials/sql/subqueries).

blocks.code: SELECT name, country FROM customers WHERE country IN ('US', 'UK');

blocks.content:
name              | country
------------------+--------
Ada Lovelace      | UK
Grace Hopper      | US
Margaret Hamilton | US

blocks.text: `x BETWEEN a AND b` is shorthand for `x >= a AND x <= b`. Both ends are included, which matters for prices and dates: `BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-31'` includes the 31st. Because dates in this database are stored as text, `BETWEEN` on dates only works when every value uses the same `YYYY-MM-DD` format.

blocks.code: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 5 AND 40;

blocks.content:
name          | price
--------------+------
Mouse pad     | 8.99
USB cable     | 12
Monitor stand | 39.5

blocks.text: `NULL` means *no value*: unknown, not applicable or not entered yet. It is not zero and not an empty string. Any comparison with NULL (`= NULL`, `<> NULL`, `> NULL`) yields *unknown* rather than true, and WHERE keeps only rows whose condition is true. So `assignee = NULL` matches nothing, even for rows where the assignee really is NULL. The correct tests are `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`:

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE tickets (
OK: INSERT INTO tickets (title, assignee) VALUES
OK: SELECT title FROM tickets WHERE assignee = NULL

title
-----------
Write docs
Update logo

blocks.text: The first SELECT found no rows, so the playground printed only `OK`; the second found both unassigned tickets.

blocks.title: = NULL never matches
blocks.text: `WHERE assignee = NULL` is valid syntax in every database and returns no rows in every database, so nothing warns you. Always write `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`. The same logic bites `NOT IN`: if the list contains a NULL, `x NOT IN (...)` is never true and the query returns nothing. Filter NULLs out of the subquery or use `NOT EXISTS` instead.

All of these operators are ordinary conditions, so they combine with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT` from the previous lesson: `WHERE category IN ('Office', 'Stationery') AND price NOT BETWEEN 5 AND 10 AND name NOT LIKE 'S%'` is a perfectly good filter.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Find the products whose name contains a space, then the customers who joined in 2024 using `BETWEEN` on the `joined` column.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: Which pattern matches names that end with `son`?
questions.explanation: The % wildcard stands for anything before the fixed ending. `'son%'` matches names that start with son, `'_son'` only four-letter names, and `'%son%'` names containing son anywhere.

questions.question: `price BETWEEN 5 AND 10` excludes products that cost exactly 10.
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends; it is equivalent to price >= 5 AND price <= 10.

seo.title: SQL LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and NULL – Filtering Operators
seo.description: Learn SQL pattern matching with LIKE wildcards, list membership with IN, inclusive ranges with BETWEEN, and why NULL needs IS NULL rather than = NULL.
